lignes.texte: It’s just another regular flight, cruising at 35,000 feet (10,668 meters). Passengers do what
they usually do: watching movies, sleeping and counting the hours until their back on the ground.
It’s a completely uneventful journey. Until a blinding white flash
obliterates the horizon. A fireball erupts in the distance.
The passengers don’t know it, but the world below them is gone…
2:45:00 P.M. ET Tony Benelli didn’t even
want to be on this flight. The sales manager from New Jersey is flying to Los Angeles for
a mandatory conference. He’s settled into seat 12A onboard United Flight 1202, adjusting his
neck pillow and noise cancelling headphones as the plane cruises over the heartland.
2:47:00 P.M. ET Tony stares at clouds
drifting lazily past his window when the sky suddenly turns a searing white.
He gasps, staring into the blinding glare for one frozen second before his reflexes force his
eyes shut. Even for elite Air Force pilots flying near nuclear test detonations in the 1950s, the
level of the brightness was unforgettable. As one described, “Shards of brilliant light penetrated
all the protective devices and severely pained my eyes for a few seconds. As the brilliance faded,
I could see the bones in my hand. Suddenly I began to feel as if millions of long,
hot needles were shooting through my body… I had the horrible sensation of being on fire.”
Tony is about 80 miles (129 km) from the epicenter of the nuclear blast, sealed inside in a
commercial Boeing 737. The distance saved his life, but it doesn’t mean he’s unscathed. The
intense flash instantly burns an afterimage in his left retina, causing a headache that will last for
hours. But in the sheer confusion of the moment, he won’t connect either symptom to the blast.
Three rows back, a grad student named Maya looked directly at the flash for 3 full seconds. Now,
she’s got her hands clamped over her eyes, convinced she’s gone permanently blind.
That’s the story of most people in aisle A, who didn’t look away fast enough.
Flash blindness from a nuclear detonation at a distance lasts up to 2 minutes in daylight,
and up to 10 at night. Maya doesn't know this. She’s sitting in the dark,
with nothing but the sheer terror of the unknown to keep her company.
As the flash fades, Tony looks down. Chicago is now a column of fire climbing
toward the edge of space. A mushroom cloud swallows everything in its path.
The city that 2.7 million people called home is nothing but a boiling wasteland.
Still dazed, Tony manages to rip off his noise-cancelling headphones. The
cabin is flooded with a sound that makes his skin crawl. 150
people are screaming at once. The realization hits them all at once.
Chicago is gone, America is on fire… and they have no idea what to do next.
2:48:00 P.M. E.T. The PA crackles to life.
Captain Jamila Okafor’s voice cuts through the screams filling the cabin. Remarkably,
she sounds calm. She tells the passengers they are making a minor routing change due
to airspace restrictions up ahead and orders them to fasten their seatbelts.
Airspace restrictions?
Tony glances back out the mushroom cloud looming over Chicago.
What Tony doesn't know is that the plane he’s currently sitting in… is flying blind.
The cockpit is a bank of dead instruments. No radar. No datalink. No ground control.
The Chicago air traffic control sector went dark right around the time a Russian RS-28
Sarmat missile, known as Satan II, completed its 28-minute arc from western Russia.
It detonated 6,500 feet (1981 meters) above Chicago’s West Adams Street.
The Chicago sector didn’t fall silent because of a technical fault. It went silent
because Chicago was vaporized. And Captain Okafor knew the minute she saw the flash.
She is already running the map in her head.
Every frequency that’s just static is a city she can’t reach.
Chicago: Wiped off the map. Denver? Dead air. Which means NORAD,
Peterson and Schriever Air Force Bases, all confirmed nuclear targets, are gone.
Kansas City? Whiteman Air Force Base, with its B-2 bombers? Probably dust.
She hasn’t dropped a hint of this to the cabin. What the passengers
also don't know is what happened in the cockpit when the flash lit up the sky.
Military nuclear bomber pilots fly with $7 million PLZT goggles, made of Polarized Lead
Zirconium Titanate. It’s a masterpiece of Cold War engineering that detects a nuclear flash and turns
opaque in a ten-millionth of a second. It’s so the people dropping the bombs don't go blind doing it.
The pilots of United Flight 1202 had nothing but a standard commercial windshield. When
Chicago was obliterated, that windshield offered zero protection. The blast seared
straight through their retinas. Right now, the aircraft is flying on autopilot,
holding the heading and altitude Okafor set before her world plunged into darkness. Her
vision begins to fight through the haze, her mind races. coming back.
2:51:00 P.M. E.T. – T+4 Minutes
The aircraft banks hard left, to the south,
fleeing the cloud and what remains of Chicago. They’re abandoning the flight
path that was supposed to take them through Iowa and Nebraska and into Denver airspace.
That route is dead.
As they bank, the mushroom cloud towering over
Lake Michigan slowly slide behind Tony’s window, shrinking against the horizon.
2:54:00 P.M. E.T. - T+7 Minutes
Tony Benelli is sitting inside a 70 ton metal tube traveling through the sky at
over 530 miles per hour (853 kph). On a normal day, this works because of a vast,
invisible web of infrastructure. 14,000 air traffic controllers,
thousands of navigation beacons, instrument landing systems, GPS satellites all work
flawlessly to keep aircraft in the sky. All because the civilization on
the ground is functioning. Today, that ground is gone.
When the warhead detonated above West Adams Street, it not only destroyed
Chicago but also sent an electromagnetic pulse outward at the speed of light. This pulse,
invisible and instantaneous, carried enough energy to find every unshielded electronic
system within its radius and burn it alive. It’s a well-documented phenomenon. In 1962,
the United States detonated a 1.4-megaton nuclear weapon almost 250 miles (400 km) above the Pacific
Ocean in a test called Starfish Prime. The EMP it produced blew out streetlights in Hawaii,
triggered burglar alarms, and took down a telephone microwave relay station… and that
was 900 miles (1448 km) from ground zero. Flight 1202 was just 80 miles (129 km) away.
Nobody onboard knows why Chicago just got vaporized. 3 days earlier, Russia
had detonated a tactical nuclear weapon over a Ukrainian military installation outside Lviv,
the first nuclear strike since 1945. Washington issued a 72 hour ultimatum.
That clock just hit zero. And Russia's reply just arrived
on American soil. 14 nuclear warheads, each one with a city’s name on it. No one believed
it was possible. No one thought Russia would actually plunge the world into a global war.
But they did…
The aircraft suddenly shudders. The shockwave from
the Chicago blast has caught up with them. It rips through the airframe,
as the sound of groaning metal fills the cabin. Passengers scream as the plane
lurches. The entire cabin violently vibrates. Then after 3 agonizing seconds… it stops.
3:01:00 P.M. E.T. -- T+14 Minutes
Tony glances at his phone, the screen is blank. He was never one to follow the
rules and had left it off airplane mode. Just a few minutes ago it had a signal and then the
networks collapsed. He stares at the screen hoping the bars will miraculously come back.
They won’t. Somewhere below,
the cell towers that would normally route his call home are either destroyed or without power.
The ones that are still standing are overwhelmed by 9 million
panicked people in the greater Chicago area simultaneously screaming into a dead network.
3:03:00 P.M. E.T. – T+16 Minutes
Every seatback monitor, every overhead display,
every single cabin light shuts down. The plane is engulfed in darkness. A second EMP blast, from a
second detonation somewhere to the southwest, has intercepted the aircraft over eastern Nebraska.
Someone in the back starts crying. Someone else starts praying.
In the cockpit, the situation is terminal. The pilots have just lost their primary
navigation display, their autopilot, their radio contact with Denver Center,
and their landing gear controls. The crew reach for the last resort.
The APU. It’s a backup gas
turbine engine in the tail designed to save the aircraft when everything else fails. The pilots
abandon their safety checks and frantically try to bring it online. Then reality hits.
Its electronic controller is digital. And the EMP got there first.
Even if it starts, it doesn’t matter. The APU powers the aircraft’s systems;
the systems need people running underneath them to
mean anything. The navigation beacons are all gone. The instrument landing
systems at every airport in range are all dark. The radio frequencies are empty.
All they have is their mechanical backup instruments: an altimeter,
an attitude indicator, and an airspeed needle.
They know the remaining fuel state, and have a rough map burned into their head.
Captain Okafor could try to find an airport in their flight path. Salt
Lake City? Denver International? But she has no way of knowing if those cities even exist
anymore. Every other major airport within her glide path sits next to a potential target. The
minor ones have runways she can’t see, with ground control crews that aren't answering.
With the automated hydraulic landing gear offline, their only hope is for the manual
emergency crank to lower the wheels. The first officer tears open the floor panel,
grips the handle and starts to crank furiously. They hear an audible groan
from underneath them. 10 turns. 20. Then… a sickening metallic snap.
The manual link shears under the strain. The handle spins loose in the first officer's hand.
Every landing, airport or otherwise, is now a belly landing. They have 70
tones of screaming metal, a cabin full of terrified passengers and no wheels.
Then the answer comes.
The eastern Colorado plains. It flashes through Captain Okafor’s mind. It’s vast,
flat and more importantly, it’s empty. It’s the kind of terrain where a heavy aircraft
with fried instruments and 150 people aboard might have a chance of survival.
3:04:00 P.M. E.T. – T+17 Minutes
After flying as long as she can, Captain Okafor reaches for the intercom.
She doesn’t tell the passengers about the utter devastation ripping across America. Instead,
she delivers a rehearsed script. The main electrical systems have failed
and they need to attempt an emergency landing. They have 30 minutes. Then
she gives the commands every passenger dreads: prepare to brace for impact.
Then she lies. Everything will be fine.
She puts the intercom down. Even she doesn’t believe that last part.
3:30:00 P.M. E.T. – T+43 Minutes
The flight crew moves through the cabin one last time. Over the panic, they shout the instructions
for the emergency landing. Shoes off, glasses off, brace for impact. Tony tightens his seatbelt and,
his hands trembling, he grips his wedding band. Outside his window, the eastern Colorado plains
stretch in every direction: flat, brown, and seemingly endless. But
towering over the horizon, the faint dark line of the Rockies is rushing forward,
getting closer with every second. 3:34:00 P.M. E.T. – T+47 Minutes
“BRACE. BRACE. BRACE.”
Tony folds forward, along with everyone else on the plane. Forehead on the seat
back. Arms locked over his head. Eyes shut tight.
He can feel the aircraft through his shoes, through the seat, through the armrests. The
whole machine is vibrating with the frequency of something moving faster than it was designed to.
He counts. One. Two. Three. Four… Contact.
An enormous grinding sound tears through the cabin as the heavy aluminum fuselage meets
the frozen earth at 198 miles per hour (319 kph). The sound doesn’t register in his ears,
it slams into his chest, his spine, his back teeth.
The overhead bins shatter. Someone screams. The violent
deceleration throws him forward into his seatbelt. It cuts into his waist,
feeling like it could snap at any moment. He grips the armrests, knuckle-white,
and grinds his teeth waiting either for the terror to stop… or for his world to go black.
Neither happens.
The engines hit the ground and shear off their mounts. At that point, the sound drops in pitch
and the aircraft feels lighter. It’s the most wrong sensation Tony has ever felt in his life.
Then physics catches up.
The airframe twists and creaks under the immense stress of the
landing. The rear section buckles and snaps. Suddenly, there is daylight behind Tony where
a bulkhead used to be. The wind rushes in… then the heat comes. A wall of fire,
lasting just 2 seconds, roars over him and speeds toward the front of the cabin.
Then, just as soon as it arrived, it dissipates and is gone.
Silence. Complete and total silence.
Tony lifts his head.
The seat in front of him is there. The seat behind him is there. Cold
air blasts through the cabin from the wrong direction, carrying the bitter stench of
Jet-A and frozen dirt. Tony grimaces as he looks back toward the rear of the aircraft.
Where row 28 used to connect to row 29, there is only sky and a jagged cross-section of aluminum.
The rear section separated when the jet hit the ground, rolling twice,
and on the second roll the center fuel tank found what it needed:
friction and heat. The fireball lasted 4 seconds. Tony felt 2 of them on the back of his neck,
along with the seared memories of a few milliseconds of anguished screams.
Flight 1202 is missing 34 passengers. Dazed and confused, Tony looks out
the window. On the southwestern horizon, something is building. A glow. Orange-white.
Enormous. Too fast and too total to be a fire, at least not one he can describe.
Peterson Air Force Base. Colorado Springs. NORAD.
The second wave of Russian warheads is landing on the horizon at the same time as Flight 1202.
Tony watches them bloom against the mountains and understands now, sitting shoeless in a broken
aircraft in a Colorado wheat field, that what he saw over Chicago was not the end of anything.
It was just the opening move.
3:36:00 P.M. E.T. – T+49 Minutes
The forward fuselage of United Flight 1202 sits splayed and
sheared, with its tail end torn open. Inside, 98 people are still trapped.
Tony is one of them.
He does a fast inventory of himself. Neck. Okay. Back. Both hands. Both feet. He’s fine,
miraculously. But then a wave of guilt hits him as he thinks
about the 34 people who disappeared in a fireball behind him moments earlier.
Around him, the cabin is a wall of sound. People are crying, screaming and shouting. A man in
row 9 prays in a language nobody recognizes. The overhead bins above
rows 26 and 27 have burst open, shedding their contents across the
seats below. Someone’s roller bag. A laptop. A child’s backpack. An unused neck pillow.
Michelle, the lead flight attendant, is already moving. She covers the length of the cabin in
20 seconds, assessing, triaging, her voice trying to cut through the noise. A doctor in
row 7 identifies herself and starts working forward from there. They meet
in the middle and begin moving row by row. A broken wrist in 11C. Concussion in 15A.
Lacerations across half the left side of the cabin where the overhead bins came down.
ThenTony looks at Row 17… and wishes he hadn’t.
A man is sitting perfectly upright in 17B with his seatbelt still fastened,
his eyes wide open. A piece of aluminum the length of a forearm embedded deep in his chest,
driven through the seat back in front of him on impact.
He’s not breathing and hasn’t been breathing since the aircraft shuddered to a stop.
A dark stain of blood is seeping through his white shirt. The woman next to him in 17A is hysterical,
screaming his name. The doctor from row 7 gets there, checks, and moves on without stopping.
Row 22 is worse.
When the rear section separated, the structural failure sent a shear wave through the floor,
buckling the cabin. A man in 22C has lost his left leg below the knee,
sliced off by a piece of aluminum shrapnel. He is conscious but he isn't screaming.
The raw shock has scrambled his nervous system. The pain hasn’t caught up yet.
The nurse from row 18 has his belt off and around the stump as an emergency tourniquet.
It takes her all of 45 seconds. She doesn’t look up. Her hands don’t shake. She is focused on the
job. A woman in 23A is missing 3 fingers on her right hand and doesn't even realize. She
calmly asks if she's ok. The nurse tells her to keep the arm elevated and moves on.
5 people in the forward section are dead. 3 from impact forces. 1 from the shard of
aluminum in row 17. And 1 elderly woman in row 25 who has no obvious injuries but no pulse.
Suddenly Tony’s gaze locks onto a set of broad shoulders, still upright in their
seat. There’s no head. Tony just stares. Saying nothing, doing nothing. The screams
of the woman sitting next to the headless passenger snap Tony out of his trance.
Tony doesn’t know what to do. He’s sitting between two mushroom clouds and a whole lot
of carnage. IHe stands up, picks up a bottle of water, and stumbles through the cabin to help.
Outside, the Colorado Springs mushroom cloud is doing what mushroom clouds do. Rising,
spreading, expanding. The second detonation means the EMP radius
has expanded. It means the fallout map has changed. Anything that was still airspace
above eastern Colorado 20 minutes ago is probably falling out of the sky.
Tony knows none of the specifics, and doesn’t care. Michelle calls the cabin to attention again,
her voice booming down the aisle. She warns the passengers that the air outside is lethal.
She orders them to stay inside the cabin. No one can touch the emergency exits. The need
to stay in place and wait it out. A voice from the back cracks, demanding to know how
long they have to wait. As long as it takes.
Back in the cockpit, Captain Okafor is staring at the horizon. She knows the prevailing winds are
carrying a toxic, radioactive fallout plume from Colorado Springs straight toward them.
An open wheat field has a Protection Factor of 1. Meaning no protection at all.
The aircraft's aluminum skin, insulation, seat mass, and the density of everything packed
into the forward fuselage adds up to something significantly better than standing in a field.
Working together, the survivors launch into a desperate survival plan. They use
part of an emergency egress slide, plastic garbage bags, duct tape,
and clothes from the overhead bins to seal the open rear of the aircraft.
There is a patchwork of sweaters, jackets, and bridesmaid dress still in its dry-cleaning bag,
and a child’s fancy dress costume that Tony doesn’t spend too long looking at.
They pack every gap. They cover bare skin. They inventory the galley. There’s still 23
large bottles of water, 400 snack packages, 14 first class meal trays that never got
served because the world ended before the flight attendants could hand them out.
It’s enough, probably. But for how long?
Tony sits on the floor of the aisle in row 12 with
his back against the seat. He glances at the mushroom cloud on the horizon.
Outside, the 7/10 rule is running whether any of the survivors know it or not. For
every sevenfold increase in time after a nuclear blast, the radiation dose rate
outside drops by a factor of 10. At 7 hours, it's one-tenth of what it was at hour 1. At 49 hours,
one-hundredth. Every hour they stay inside this makeshift shelter, the math moves in their favor.
Midnight – T+8 Hours 26 Minutes
Eastern Colorado in February drops to 18 degrees (-7.8 Celsius) overnight.
A commercial aircraft fuselage is designed to be pressurized and heated by systems that
run on electricity. United Flight 1202 has none. The insulation in the cabin walls,
just 2 inches (5 cm) of fiberglass batting behind the interior panels,
slows the heat loss. But it does not stop it.
By midnight the cabin temperature is 38 degrees (3.3 Celsius)
To survive the freezing dark, the passengers are forced to adapt. They huddle together,
just like the Andes plane crash survivors did in 1972. They piled together, sharing their
body heat, using every piece of clothing not sealing a fuselage gap as insulation.
The dead, meanwhile, remain in their seats. The man in 17B is still upright, still seatbelted,
still with the piece of aluminum in his chest. The 4 in the forward section are covered.
The 34 in the rear section are still a mangled,
charred heap 600 feet (183 meters) away, buried under the frost that’s
forming on the blackened aluminium. 3:00 A.M. – T+11 Hours 26 Minutes
The cabin temperature is 29 degrees (-1.7 Celsius). Tony’s breath hangs in the frozen air.
The man in 22C, the one who lost his leg below the knee, is running a dangerous fever. The nurse
sits with him through the night, monitoring, adjusting the tourniquet, and holding his hand.
He was supposed to be flying home for his brother’s wedding and jokes the crash will
make a great best man speech. The nurse smiles back and nods her head. She doesn’t have the heart
to tell it’s a speech he’ll never live to make. Tony tries to sleep. It’s pointless. He drifts
in and out, too cold and too uncomfortable to fully lose consciousness. He thinks about
his wife. He thinks about the man in 17B. He thinks about the 34 in the field and then stops.
There’s a limit to how much suffering someone can think of.
4:00 A.M. - T+12 Hours 26 Minutes
A child 2 rows back starts crying. Her mother holds her
close and whispers something soothing until the cabin falls quiet again.
Sometime after 4 a.m., the nurse notices something wrong. The woman in seat 23C has
stopped breathing. She's a 58 year old kindergarten teacher from Naperville,
Illinois. She had helped pack clothing into the fuselage gaps,
shared her blanket with the child 2 rows back, and fell asleep sometime around
midnight with no visible injuries. But she was a dead woman walking.
The forces of the initial impact had ruptured her spleen on contact. Internal bleeding, masked
by a surge of adrenaline, did its work behind the abdominal wall. As the hours passed, blood
pooled in her body cavity. Her blood pressure dropped slowly. Eventually, her brain received
less and less oxygen and decided to shut down. The nurse checks her pulse twice and places
a blanket over her. Then she moves on…
6:50 A.M. – T+15 Hours 16 Minutes
Dawn comes gray and thin through the condensation filled windows.
Michelle is already awake, doing her job. She has been on her feet for the better
part of 16 hours straight with zero sleep. She checks the man missing part of his leg
first. His fever broke sometime before 4 a.m. The nurse is still fast asleep in the
seat beside him, still holding his hand. Tony stands up. Every muscle and bone in
his body screams in agony. He knows if he makes it out of this field,
it’ll take weeks to recover. He looks down at his feet and finds a bag of
crushed pretzels. He picks them up and puts them in his jacket pocket.
Mid-Morning – T+~19 Hours
Michelle opens the forward door later that day. The cold air rushes in finding every gap
in Tony’s clothing immediately. It carries the stench of thawing dirt and acrid jet
fuel. But underneath is a faint chemical tang. Tony tries not to think about it,
remembering the glowing mushroom cloud that bloomed over the horizon the day before.
The survivors stagger out onto the wing skin and down to the churned up wheat stubble. Looking down
the length of the Rockies to the southwest, a gray-brown stain sits below the blue at
the horizon where Colorado Springs used to be. To the north, somewhere distant, was Chicago.
Tony glances back to the tail section. The field is scorched in a rough circle from the fireball,
a charred resting place for the 34 people who lost their lives.
The remaining passengers turn east, toward the vacant farmhouse 3 miles (4.8 km) away with the
well that probably still works. Tony places a hand in his jacket pocket and feels the soft
rustle of the pretzel packet. Then they all start walking.
One step. Then the next.
What would happen if you were trapped in your neighborhood when the bombs
started to fall? Watch “World War 3 - Hour by Hour in the Suburbs”
to see how the apocalypse unfolds closer to home. Or click on this.
